notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 22, drawn from the sources I was able to consult.

---

## Ezekiel 22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

Ellicott notes the chapter consists of three short prophecies: (1) vv.2–16 recount Jerusalem’s sins, with reference back to chapter 18; (2) vv.17–22 depict punishment and purification under the figure of melting metals in a furnace; (3) vv.23–31 return to sins not mentioned in the first section, showing corruption pervades all classes, and closes with certain punishment. The chapter as a whole is a justification of the divine judgment. [Ellicott, studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)

JFB similarly says the chapter repeats charges from chapter 20, but whereas chapter 20 was a historical review, here the *present* sins of the nation are brought forward. [JFB, biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 1 — "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying…"

A standard prophetic introduction marking a new oracle. No commentator consulted treats this verse separately from v. 2.

---

### v. 2 — "As for you, son of man, will you judge her? Will you pass judgment on the city of bloodshed? Then confront her with all her abominations"

- **"Will you judge, will you judge"**: The repetition of the verb is for emphasis (cf. Ezek. 20:4). Ezekiel acts as both prosecutor and judge on Yahweh’s behalf. The sense is, "Will you not judge?" (JFB). The margin reading "plead for" is not appropriate here. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html); [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"The bloody city"** (lit. "city of bloods"): Named for murders perpetrated in her, including child sacrifices to Molech. Jerusalem is no longer "the holy city" or "God’s special city" — she is the *bloody city*. Ezekiel seems to borrow the phrase from Nahum 3:1, who had arraigned Nineveh as "the bloody city" par excellence — Jerusalem had become as bad as Nineveh. [EnduringWord (Guzik)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/); [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"Confront her with all her abominations"**: God commands Ezekiel to lay out the charges publicly, not to hide the extent of sin. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 3 — "O city who brings her own doom by shedding blood within her walls and making idols to defile herself"

- **"That her time may come"**: Her time of punishment. The inevitable consequence is presented as if it were her own purpose — she has been so fully warned that continuing in sin seems to involve a deliberate design of bringing on judgment. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- **"Making idols … to defile herself"**: Instead of deriving advantage from idolatrous sacrifices, she only brought on herself "the time" of her punishment. The idols were made "against herself" (Prov. 8:36). [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"Within her walls"**: Poole notes that the murders were aggravated because they occurred where so many were present who should have provided safety to the innocent — "it was not done in a wilderness." [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 4 — "you are guilty of the blood you have shed … you have brought your days to a close … I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the lands"

- **"Your days … your years"**: The "days" refer to the shorter period of the siege; the "years" to the longer period of the captivity. Together they express that Jerusalem is ripe for punishment. The Rabbinical commentators interpreted the "days" as the destruction of Jerusalem and the "years" as the Babylonian captivity. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- **"A reproach … a mockery"**: This is the inevitable result of the contrast between high profession and inconsistent performance. Israel’s law stood far above any other nation’s, but the people utterly disregarded it — just as Paul later said, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you" (Rom. 2:24). The Jews especially exposed themselves to derision by claiming to be God’s chosen people with universal dominion, contrasted with their overthrow. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- Matthew Henry summarizes: Jerusalem has filled the measure of her sins. Those who give themselves to be ruled by their lusts will justly be given up to be portioned by them. [MHC](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 5 — "Those near and far will mock you, O infamous city, full of turmoil"

- **"Infamous"**: The margin reads "polluted in name." The nations mockingly call her "thou polluted one … and full of confusion" (Fairbairn), referring to the tumultuous violence within. A sad contrast to the Jerusalem once called "the holy city." [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"Full of turmoil"** (KJV "much vexed"): Refers to the internal confusion, commotions, and social disorders of the decaying kingdom. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)

---

### v. 6 — "See how every prince of Israel within you has used his power to shed blood"

- **"Every prince … to his power"** (lit. "each according to his arm"): The rulers, who should have preserved order and administered justice, were foremost in deeds of violence. They made their own arm of might their only law. Guzik notes that instead of using power in ways that honor God and serve His people, they used it in violent, self-serving ways. Judicial murders are intended (cf. 2 Kings 21:16; 24:4). [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html); [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 7 — "Father and mother are treated with contempt … the foreign resident is exploited, the fatherless and the widow are oppressed"

- These are transgressions of specific divine commands: filial respect (Lev. 19:32; 20:9), care for strangers (Ex. 22:21; Deut. 24:14), and protection of the fatherless and widow (Ex. 22:22-24). [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- Guzik adds: "The Jews were commanded to honor their fathers and mothers (Ex. 20:12), and so are believers today (Eph. 6:1–3). God even attached a special promise to this commandment — 'that your days may be long upon the land' — and now the Jews were about to be exiled from their land" (Wiersbe). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 8 — "You have despised My holy things and profaned My Sabbaths"

- The plural "Sabbaths" extends beyond the weekly Sabbath to sacred days and years as well. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- These sins were not only against the community but against God Himself. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)

---

### v. 9 — "Among you are slanderous men bent on bloodshed; within you are those who eat on the mountain shrines and commit acts of indecency"

- **"Slanderous men"** (KJV "men that carry tales"): Informers who by misrepresentations cause innocent blood to be shed (Lev. 19:16). Literally, "one who goes to and fro as a merchant." [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"Eat on the mountain shrines"**: Joining in idol sacrifices, a sin often reproved by the prophets. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)

---

### v. 10 — "In you they have uncovered the nakedness of their fathers; in you they violate women during their menstrual impurity"

- **"Uncovered their fathers’ nakedness"**: Refers to incest with a father’s wife (cf. Lev. 18:7-8). [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"Violate women during menstrual impurity"**: A double sin — not only sexual violation but doing so during a woman’s menstrual period, which was specifically forbidden (Lev. 18:19; 20:18). "In their excesses they acted more like beasts than creatures of reason" (Feinberg). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 11 — "One man commits an abomination with his neighbor’s wife; another wickedly defiles his daughter-in-law; and yet another violates his sister, his own father’s daughter"

- All these sexual sins are specifically forbidden in Leviticus 18. The list covers adultery, incest with a daughter-in-law, and incest with a sister. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- The comprehensive nature of the sexual corruption shows a society that has abandoned all moral restraint. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 12 — "In you they take bribes to shed blood. You engage in usury, take excess interest, and extort your neighbors. But Me you have forgotten, declares the Lord GOD"

- The final area of sin: financial exploitation — bribery leading to judicial murder, usury, and extortion. All these had been constantly denounced by the law and the prophets. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- **"But Me you have forgotten"**: This is at once the root of all these sins and in itself the climax of all. "When one forgets God and leaves his ways, the path into every kind of abomination opens before him" (Alexander). Matthew Henry agrees: "Unmindfulness of God was at the bottom of all this wickedness. Sinners provoke God because they forget him." [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/); [MHC](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 13 — "Now look, I strike My hands together against your unjust gain and against the blood you have shed in your midst"

- **"I strike My hands together"** (KJV "I have smitten mine hand"): A gesture of indignant vengeance (cf. Ezek. 21:17). God expresses His fierce opposition to dishonest profit and bloodshed. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 14 — "Will your courage endure or your hands be strong in the day I deal with you? I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will act"

- God appeals to clear logic: can they withstand His judgment? "The Babylonians are but men, but I the Lord your God, whom you have provoked, am with them; they are my weapons of war and I strike by them" (Poole). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- The rhetorical question underscores that no human strength can endure when God Himself acts in judgment. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 15 — "I will disperse you among the nations and scatter you throughout the lands; I will purge your uncleanness"

- The scattering (exile) has a purpose: "I will consume thy filthiness out of thee." The object of God in scattering the Jews was purification. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- F.B. Meyer (quoted at Precept Austin) draws a devotional application: "We are refined by fire. Fire is pain … But God appoints it. As much as the process of refining implies the presence of the refiner, the afflictions of the believer imply the presence and purpose of the Lord." [Precept Austin / F.B. Meyer](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-f_b_meyer)

---

### v. 16 — "And when you have defiled yourself in the eyes of the nations, then you will know that I am the LORD"

- **"Defiled yourself"** (KJV "take thine inheritance in thyself"): The meaning is that through their own misconduct they forfeit the privileges of a holy nation and become profaned in the sight of the heathen. Formerly Israel was God’s inheritance; now, full of guilt, she is no longer God’s but her own — and the heathen see this. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html); [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"Then you will know that I am the LORD"**: "Thou shalt know me by my punishments, whom thou wouldst not know by my benefits" (Trapp, cited by Guzik). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 17–22 — The Furnace of Judgment (Overview)

This second oracle uses the metaphor of ancient metallurgy. Israel, once regarded as precious silver, has become a worthless compound of dross and base metals. YHWH will gather them into Jerusalem as into a furnace to melt them. The figure is used also in Isaiah 1:25; Jeremiah 6:29-30; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3. Ellicott notes the striking image: in refining silver, the process is complete when the dross separates and the refiner’s image is reflected in the molten surface. The punishment is for the purpose of purification. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)

---

### v. 18 — "the house of Israel has become dross to Me. All of them are copper, tin, iron, and lead inside the furnace; they are but the dross of silver"

- **"Dross"**: Israel has degenerated from good to bad (Isa. 1:22). They are not merely corrupt but a worthless compound of dross from silver mixed with baser metals — absolutely useless. The mixture represents the Mosaic Covenant mixed with Egyptian and Canaanite idolatry. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- Matthew Henry: "Sinners, especially backsliding professors, are, in God’s account, useless and fit for nothing." [MHC](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 19 — "I will gather you into Jerusalem"

- Jerusalem is represented as the refining pot into which the people were to be cast — their national centre, and also the centre of the war by which they were carried into captivity. Gill notes that people fled from the countryside into Jerusalem thinking it would be safe, but God’s design in this providence was their destruction there. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html); [Gill / StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/22-19.html)

---

### v. 20 — "Just as one gathers silver, copper, iron, lead, and tin into the furnace to melt with a fiery blast, so I will gather you in My anger and wrath, leave you there, and melt you"

- God will "blow on the fire" — as a refiner intensifies the heat by blowing on the coals, so God will intensify His judgment. "Ye must be put in the furnace, and subjected to the most intense fire, till your impurities are consumed away. No ordinary means will avail any thing; the most violent must be resorted to" (Clarke, cited by Guzik). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- **"I will leave you there"** is better translated "I will cast you in." [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)

---

### v. 21–22 — "I will gather you together and blow on you with the fire of My wrath … As silver is melted in a furnace, so you will be melted within the city"

- The repeated "I will gather" and "you will be melted" emphasizes the certainty and totality of the judgment. Yet there is a glimmer of hope: a refiner melts silver not to destroy it but to purify it. The judgment, though severe, aims at purification and restoration. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- Matthew Henry: "When God brings his own people into the furnace, he sits by them as the refiner by his gold, to see that they are not continued there any longer than is fitting and needful. The dross shall be wholly separated, and the good metal purified." [MHC](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"Then you will know that I, the LORD, have poured out My wrath upon you"**: The recognition formula — knowledge of Yahweh comes through the experience of His judgment. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 23–31 — Third Oracle: Corruption of All Classes

From v. 23 to the end, God shows the general corruption of all ranks. JFB structures it: prophets (v. 25), priests (v. 26), princes (v. 27), prophets again (v. 28), and the common people (v. 29). The prophets are mentioned first because their bad influence extended the widest. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 24 — "In the day of indignation, you are a land that has not been cleansed, upon which no rain has fallen"

- A difficult verse. The most probable view is that it speaks of the land as neglected and uncared for — stones not gathered, weeds allowed to grow. It has had neither human care nor the divine blessing of rain. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- JFB takes "not cleansed" as "not cleared or cultivated" — a scene of desolation, emblematic of the moral wilderness state of the people. "Nor rained upon" is a mark of divine indignation, since the early and latter rain was one of the great covenant blessings (Joel 2:23). [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- Feinberg (cited by Guzik): "According to Old Testament promise rain was one of the blessings in the material realm which attended a walk of obedience. It was withheld to turn their hearts back to the Lord." [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 25 — "The conspiracy of the princes in her midst is like a roaring lion tearing its prey"

- Note: The BSB says "princes" here but KJV/NKJV have "prophets." JFB and Ellicott read "prophets," noting they conspired both to propagate error and to oppose God’s true messengers. The "conspiracy" is a contrivance among them to "speak all alike flattering, smooth words, and give out promises of peace and safety, when there was no peace" (Poole, cited by Guzik). [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- **"They have made many widows"**: The false prophets were directly responsible for multiplying widows because husbands went to battle against Babylon, deceived by the prophets' lies and flatteries (Feinberg). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 26 — "Her priests do violence to My law and profane My holy things. They make no distinction between the holy and the common … They disregard My Sabbaths, so that I am profaned among them"

- The priests, whose "lips should have kept knowledge" (Mal. 2:7), instead did violence to the law — not merely transgressing it but wresting it to wrong ends and putting wrong constructions on it. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"No distinction between holy and profane … clean and unclean"**: One of the priests' primary duties was to teach the people these distinctions (Lev. 10:10-11; Deut. 33:10). They failed both in their own observance and in teaching the people. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html); [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- **"I am profaned among them"**: God was dishonored among His own priests when He should have been glorified. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 27 — "Her officials within her are like wolves tearing their prey, shedding blood, and destroying lives for dishonest gain"

- The princes (officials), who should have used their position for the people’s welfare, made "gain" their sole aim. "Wolves" is a notorious image for fierce, ravening cruelty (cf. Mic. 3:2-3, 9-11; John 10:12). [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- When leaders should have been faithful shepherds, they were vicious wolves — their interest was not God’s glory or the people’s welfare but dishonest gain. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 28 — "Her prophets whitewash these deeds by false visions and lying divinations, saying, 'This is what the Lord GOD says,' when the LORD has not spoken"

- **"Whitewash"** (KJV "daubed them with untempered mortar"): Refers to false assurances of peace — telling the people they need not submit to Babylon (cf. Ezek. 13:10; Jer. 6:14; 23:16-17). The false visions and lying divinations were like a wall made with mortar that had no cement — it looked nice but had no strength and could never stand. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- Nothing could have provided a more plausible excuse for the people to disobey God than an opposing "Thus saith the Lord." [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- "They were meticulous about claiming the same divine authority as the true prophets, even using the same sacred formula 'Thus saith the Lord,' but the Lord had no relation to their claims or messages" (Feinberg). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

### v. 29 — "The people of the land have practiced extortion and committed robbery. They have oppressed the poor and needy and have exploited the foreign resident without justice"

- The common people are mentioned last, after those in office. Corruption had spread downwards through the whole community. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- They imitated the behavior of their leaders, preying upon each other and those weaker. "The people of the land were the prominent land-owning citizens … often officers in the army, and they fell right in line with the princes and priests" (Wiersbe). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- **"The stranger"** (foreign resident): Israelites were commanded to remember they themselves had been "strangers in Egypt" (Ex. 22:21; 23:9). The stranger ought to have been won to Yahweh’s worship by kindness, not alienated by oppression. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 30 — "I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one"

This is the most discussed verse in the chapter.

- **"Make up the hedge / repair the wall"**: An image for leading the people to repentance and restoring moral defenses. It connects back to the false, weak wall of the false prophets (v. 28). God looked for a man to bring true strength, stability, and security. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm); [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- **"Stand in the gap before Me"**: An image for intercessory prayer, drawn from Psalm 106:23, where Moses "stood in the breach." The man God sought would, like Abraham (Gen. 20:7), Moses (Ex. 32:9-14), and David (2 Sam. 24:15-18), stand between a holy God and His sinful people through prayer. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/); [Gill / biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/22.htm)
- **"I found no one"**: A shocking statement. It does not mean there was literally no righteous person — Jeremiah, Baruch, and others were still in Jerusalem. But (JFB explains) Jeremiah had been forbidden to pray for the people (Jer. 11:14) as they were doomed to wrath. None of the godly, knowing the desperate state of the people and God’s purpose, was willing longer to interpose. And none *among the classes just listed* (vv. 25–29) was morally able for such an office. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- Ellicott similarly says: "It is not meant that there was not a single godly man, but not one of such a pure, strong, and commanding character that his intercessions might avert the threatened doom." [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)
- **Christological application**: Guzik (EnduringWord) draws a gospel connection: "Fortunately, God did find a Man to stand in the gap. This is a powerful description of Jesus and His work for His people. He is the wall of strength, stability, and security for God’s people. He is the one who ever lives to pray for His people (Hebrews 7:25). God found no one in Ezekiel’s day, but in Jesus Christ has provided this ultimate wall-builder and Man in the gap." This Christological reading is common across many evangelical traditions. [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes: "The land might be said to perish for the lack of such interpositions as saved their forefathers when Moses 'stood in the gap.' This was a proof of the general corruption, that there was not in the city sufficient righteousness to save it from utter destruction. Prince, prophet, priest, all fail." [Pulpit, via biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/22-30.htm)
- Matthew Henry: "It bodes ill to a people when judgments are breaking in upon them, and the spirit of prayer is restrained." [MHC](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/22.htm)

---

### v. 31 — "So I have poured out My indignation upon them and consumed them with the fire of My fury. I have brought their ways down upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD"

- The triple "I have" expresses judgment so certain that Ezekiel presents it as already accomplished (Feinberg). [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)
- **"Their own way have I recompensed upon their heads"**: A principle of divine justice repeated throughout Ezekiel (cf. 9:10; 11:21; 16:43; Prov. 1:31; Isa. 3:11). God gives sinners what their own deeds deserve. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)
- Morgan (cited by Guzik): "He then concluded by describing the utter hopelessness of the case. There was no man to stand in the gap, therefore the fire of wrath must proceed on its way." [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Given search limitations, full denominational comparisons are limited, but several distinct readings can be noted from the sources consulted:

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The JFB commentary (staunchly Reformed) emphasizes God’s sovereignty in judgment — the "time" of punishment arrives by divine decree. On v. 30, JFB carefully explains that "I found none" does not mean there were no believers at all (Jeremiah, Baruch were there), but that God had sovereignly forbidden intercession (Jer. 11:14) and none *among the corrupt classes listed* was morally capable. This preserves Reformed teaching on divine sovereignty and the remnant. [JFB](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/22.htm)

### Baptist
The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** (on StudyLight) on v. 30 notes the Lord sought a man "to turn the people back from sin, as Moses had once done … But He found no man! How forlorn, hopeless! … And now it was too late, Jeremiah 11:14; Jeremiah 14:1-17; Proverbs 1:26-31; Genesis 18:23." This emphasizes the point at which repentance becomes impossible — a note sometimes sounded in Baptist preaching on the "day of grace." [Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-22.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
David Guzik (EnduringWord), from a Calvary Chapel / charismatic-adjacent background, draws strong devotional and Christological application. On v. 30 he sees Jesus as the ultimate "Man in the gap." On the furnace passage (vv. 17–22), Guzik emphasizes that the fire is *purifying*, not merely destroying — "when the refiner melts the silver it isn't to destroy it, but to purify it." He also applies the false prophets' "conspiracy" (v. 25) as a warning against contemporary false prophets who "take instead of give." [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-22/)

### Anglican
Ellicott (1878, Anglican bishop) gives measured, historically-grounded exegesis. He stresses that the mockery Jerusalem suffered was "the necessary result in all ages of the contrast between high professions and inconsistent performance" — a moral warning about the hindrance to the spread of the Gospel from the unworthy lives of professing Christians. [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-22.html)

### Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness
No specific Wesleyan commentary on this chapter was retrieved within search limits. Matthew Henry (a Puritan whose works are widely used across traditions) emphasizes the refining/purifying purpose of affliction, which resonates strongly with Wesleyan holiness teaching about sanctification through trials. Henry: "When God brings his own people into the furnace, he sits by them as the refiner by his gold … The dross shall be wholly separated, and the good metal purified." [MHC](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/22.htm)
